# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out. Without atmospheric circulation, this divide would render most of the planet uninhabitable.

However, atmospheres and oceans act as powerful climate equalizers. Winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures on both sides. On ocean worlds, currents perform similar work, potentially keeping the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night—within habitable temperature ranges. Climate models suggest that planets with dense atmospheres, like those with thick CO₂ envelopes, could maintain liquid water across much of their surface.

The terminator zone deserves special attention. This permanent twilight band may offer the most temperate conditions, potentially serving as a "eyeball Earth" ring of habitability around an otherwise hostile world. Precipitation patterns concentrate here, as evaporated dayside moisture condenses over cooler regions.
